title: Does Deterministic Generate–Validate–Repair Reduce Unsafe LLM‑Generated Network Changes? A Confirmatory Paired Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed a sealed paired confirmatory study (n = 200 intent→configuration tasks) to measure whether a deterministic generate–validate–repair (GVR) pipeline that consults a deterministic NetOps validator reduces validator‑detected unsafe or semantically incorrect network changes relative to an LLM‑only generation pipeline. The run used gpt‑5‑mini with adapter‑enforced shared‑initial generation and a primary deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5). Execution consumed 200 model calls (one shared initial generation per task); no repair calls were issued because every initial candidate passed the validator. Paired contingency: n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0; estimated paired difference = 0.0; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; 95% bootstrap percentile CI = [0.0, 0.0] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). Because the baseline validator‑detected unsafe incidence was 0% on this task bank, the preregistered ≥50% relative‑reduction hypothesis could not be meaningfully evaluated. We report the preregistered design, concrete execution accounting, representative diagnostics, contamination‑check evidence (Mininet 10% holdout → 20 tasks; zero disagreements), and an artifact‑grounded discussion of operational implications and threats to validity (preregistration id: cnsms2026-gvr-effectiveness-02).

sections.introduction:
Automating intent→configuration translation with generative language models promises operational productivity gains for network operations but raises safety concerns: incorrect configurations can cause outages, violate policy, or degrade service. A commonly proposed mitigation architecture is generate–validate–repair (GVR): an LLM generates a candidate configuration, a deterministic validator checks it for syntactic and semantic violations, and the LLM is asked to repair any validator‑detected issues before deployment. The practical value of such guarded pipelines depends on (i) how often the generator produces validator‑detectable failures; (ii) the validator’s coverage and fidelity; and (iii) the repair budget and effectiveness.

This work tests a narrowly scoped, preregistered confirmatory question: Does an automated GVR pipeline that consults a deterministic NetOps validator materially reduce the incidence of validator‑detected unsafe or semantically incorrect network changes relative to an LLM‑only pipeline on a curated 200‑task intent→configuration bank? To isolate the marginal effect of adding a deterministic validator+repair to the same LLM output we preregistered and enforced shared‑initial generation semantics (one deterministic initial candidate produced per task, reused for both conditions). Our contributions are (1) a sealed preregistered paired design (n = 200) with shared‑initial semantics to isolate repair effects, (2) a fully archived autonomous execution with deterministic reconciliation and concrete accounting (completed pairs = 200, model_calls_used = 200, repair_calls = 0), and (3) an honest, artifact‑grounded null/degenerate confirmatory outcome together with operational recommendations and threats to validity grounded in the archived artifacts.
sections.related_work: Prior empirical and survey work establishes three relevant points. First, LLMs produce factual errors and exhibit prompt sensitivity and non‑determinism across domains; mitigation strategies include grounding (RAG), verifier‑assisted repair loops, and constrained agent architectures. Second, prototypes have demonstrated feasibility of intent→configuration translation using LLMs, often coupled with deterministic checkers or simulators, but instrumented production‑like failure‑rate studies are scarce. Third, agentic and tool‑enabled LLM workflows increase attack surface: red‑team and configuration‑brittleness studies document tool‑description injection and cross‑tool ambiguity that can change safety outcomes. These prior findings motivate externally auditable, preregistered measurements that isolate the marginal effect of adding deterministic repair for a fixed model and prompt policy. Our study situates itself among generator→validator→repair proposals and external‑evaluation critiques by executing a prespecified paired estimand under tightly controlled, archived conditions.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and inferential plan. The study was preregistered as cnsms2026-gvr-effectiveness-02. Design: paired binary comparison on n = 200 tasks; one shared initial generation per task (deterministic sampling policy) reused for both conditions to remove per‑condition sampling variance; one automated repair call allowed if the primary validator reported violations (repair budget = 1). The primary estimand was the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline (proportion of tasks that transition from unsafe under baseline to safe under GVR). Primary inferential test: exact McNemar two‑sided (α = 0.05). Confidence intervals for the paired difference used a bootstrap percentile method with 10,000 resamples and bootstrap_seed = 1729. The preregistration explicitly planned model_calls up to 400 (200 initial + up to 200 repair) and deterministic stopping/exclusion rules; that plan was frozen before any model calls.

Task bank and validators. We used a curated, machine‑checkable intent→configuration bank of 200 tasks spanning four topology clusters (enterprise, campus, datacenter, edge; 50 tasks each). Each task encodes initial and expected final states, workflow constraints (examples: make‑before‑break, must_be_down_for_fields), and an explicit required_sequence. The primary deterministic checker deterministic_netops_validator_v5 enforces intent/constraint rules and emits structured diagnostics (valid flag, violation codes, parsed_command_count, required_command_count). A Mininet‑based data‑plane emulator was preregistered as a secondary disagreement detector and applied to a randomized 10% holdout (20 tasks) to detect validator–emulator mismatches.

Model, generation semantics, and adapter enforcement. The experiment used the hosted model declared in the preregistration (gpt‑5‑mini) invoked via the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter. Crucially, the adapter enforced shared_initial generation semantics: for each task the system produced a single initial candidate (deterministic sampling) which was reused for both baseline (LLM‑only) and guarded (GVR) conditions. This isolates the effect of validator+repair on the same generator output and removes per‑condition sampling variance. Adapter accounting reports hosted_model_call_event_count = 200 and stage_counts = {shared_initial_generation: 200}.

Repair policy, budgets, and contamination handling. The preregistered repair policy allowed one automated repair prompt to the same LLM per task when the primary validator reported violations. The contamination_plan deterministically excluded tasks where primary validator vs emulator disagreed; predetermined sensitivity analyses would include flagged tasks as failures or successes for robustness checks. Missingness/exclusion rules were fixed in advance and applied deterministically during execution.
sections.results:
Execution accounting. The autonomous run completed all planned episodes: completed_episode_count = 400 (shared initial generation reused across conditions) and complete_pair_count = 200. Model_calls_used = 200 (one shared initial generation per task); no repair calls were issued. Condition summaries (analysis/condition_summary.csv) show baseline successes = 200/200 and guarded successes = 200/200 (success_rate = 1.0 for both). The paired contingency table (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv) is: n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0.

Primary inferential result. With zero discordant pairs the observed paired difference estimate = 0.0. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. The bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples; seed = 1729) is [0.0, 0.0]. Under the preregistered estimand and test the prespecified ≥50% relative‑reduction hypothesis is logically untestable on this sample because there were no baseline validator failures for GVR to reduce.

Repair activity, contamination checks, and diagnostics. Because no initial candidate failed deterministic_netops_validator_v5, the GVR pipeline applied zero repair prompts and incurred zero repair‑call cost. The preregistered Mininet holdout (10% → 20 tasks) executed; the analysis artifact analysis/contamination_summary.csv reports zero validator–emulator disagreements. Deterministic reconciliation artifacts report all consistency checks passed (pair_accounting_consistent = true, episode_accounting_consistent = true). Representative task artifacts (e.g., pair‑000001..pair‑000006) show shared initial generator outputs that matched the required_sequence and passed validation (validator_trace.validation_after.valid = true and violation_count = 0). Representative difficulty annotations indicate that tasks exercised medium‑to‑very_hard workflow constraints despite generating validator‑satisfying candidates.

Planned sensitivity branches not invoked. Several preregistered sensitivity analyses (treating flagged contamination tasks as failures/successes, alternative missingness treatments) were not invoked because no tasks were flagged and no episodes failed. Secondary estimands (average repair iterations, GVR‑introduced failure rate, model‑call cost per successful repair) are uncomputed because no repair attempts occurred; secondary_results are recorded as empty in the analysis bundle.

Reproducibility gap. All major execution artifacts are archived; however, the explicit randomized selection seed used for the Mininet holdout is not present as a labeled artifact, which prevents exact reconstruction of the drawn holdout despite the contamination summary evidence of zero disagreements. We report this gap transparently as preregistered and archived evidence shows the holdout executed and produced zero disagreements.
sections.discussion:
Conditional interpretation and operational meaning. The degenerate confirmatory outcome demonstrates a straightforward logical point: when the chosen model, prompt policy, and adapter produce validator‑passing candidates for every item in a workload, adding a validator‑coupled automated repair step cannot reduce validator‑detected failures. This null result is narrow and conditional; it does not imply GVR is universally unhelpful. Rather, it shows that GVR’s marginal operational benefit depends on baseline validator failure prevalence and validator coverage.

Why baseline failures were zero in this run. Artifact‑grounded explanations include: (1) the prompt template and deterministic shared_initial semantics produced candidates that conformed to the explicit task‑bank constraints; (2) the curated task bank encodes clear required_sequences that map directly to validator checks and may therefore be easier for a deterministic prompt policy to satisfy than more ambiguous, real‑world intents; (3) the primary validator enforces the task‑encoded constraints but may omit device‑level or vendor idiosyncratic behaviors detectable only by an emulator or real device; and (4) the single repair budget combined with shared_initial design removes per‑condition re‑sampling as a pathway for generating alternative, repairable candidates.

Operational recommendations. Before investing in automated repair automation, practitioners should (a) measure baseline validator failure prevalence on representative workload distributions; (b) evaluate validator coverage using end‑to‑end emulation or staged device testing; (c) consider extending validator semantics to include richer device models and vendor idiosyncrasies; and (d) explore multi‑sample or multi‑model generation policies and larger repair budgets when baseline failures are nontrivial. When baseline validator failures are rare, resources may be more effectively applied to improving validator fidelity, adversarial testing, or human‑in‑the‑loop approval pathways. Conversely, when baseline failures are common, a well‑designed GVR pipeline with sufficient repair budget can reduce validator‑detectable issues.

Threats to validity. Internal validity: preregistration, deterministic adapter enforcement, and frozen stopping rules protect against post‑hoc design changes; however, shared_initial design trades generality for control and removes per‑condition sampling variance. Construct validity: the primary validator checks task‑encoded constraints but may omit device‑level or vendor idiosyncratic failure modes only visible under end‑to‑end execution. External validity: evaluation used a single hosted model (gpt‑5‑mini), a single sampling policy (shared initial), and a curated task bank; results may differ across model families, sampling temperatures, multiple draws, larger repair budgets, adversarial inputs, or production workloads. Conclusion validity: the McNemar test is uninformative when discordant pairs are zero; nevertheless reporting zero‑discordance is an operationally meaningful datum that should inform future workload selection and power planning.

Directions for follow‑on empirical work. Artifact‑grounded extensions include (i) repeating the preregistered paired protocol on workload draws with empirically measured nonzero baseline validator failure rates, (ii) increasing repair budget (multi‑step repair) and permitting per‑condition resampling to estimate marginal gains from re‑generation, (iii) broadening validator fidelity with richer emulator/device checks and measuring validator–emulator disagreement rates, and (iv) evaluating multi‑model ensembles or stochastic sampling (temperature > 0) to quantify how generator diversity interacts with validator/repair effectiveness.
sections.conclusion: We preregistered and ran a sealed paired study comparing LLM‑only generation to a deterministic GVR pipeline on 200 NetOps intent→configuration tasks using gpt‑5‑mini and deterministic_netops_validator_v5. Both pipelines produced validator‑passing configurations for every task (n11 = 200; no discordant pairs). The preregistered hypothesis of a ≥50% relative reduction in validator‑detected unsafe changes was untestable because the baseline failure rate was 0%. This outcome emphasizes that the marginal value of automated repair is workload dependent: when baseline validator failures are rare, repair yields no measured benefit for validator‑detected errors. Future work should evaluate GVR on workloads with nontrivial baseline failure prevalence, extend validator fidelity with richer emulator or device checks, explore multi‑sample and multi‑model generation policies, and study multi‑step or human‑in‑the‑loop repair strategies. All execution artifacts, logs, and analysis outputs are archived for independent inspection (preregistration id: cnsms2026-gvr-effectiveness-02).

disclosure_statement: Disclosure (mandatory). This study executed under the autonomous post‑lock preregistration cnsms2026-gvr-effectiveness-02. Declared model: gpt‑5‑mini (provider label: openai_responses) invoked via the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter family. The exact initial master prompt is archived at provenance/master_prompt.txt (SHA‑256: 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba). Topic constraints: the human Research Director limited the study to Generative AI and LLMs for NetOps focusing on safety/reliability of generated network changes. Frameworks and tools: code and experiment orchestration used the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 framework and the deterministic task generator deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5. Primary deterministic validator: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (intent/constraint checks). A Mininet‑based emulator served as the preregistered secondary disagreement detector applied to a randomized 10% holdout (20 tasks). Preregistration and freeze: the experimental plan (estimand, sample size n = 200, paired design, stopping rules, max model calls = 400, repair call budget = 1 per task, shared‑initial generation semantics) was frozen before any model calls. Autonomous execution and artifacts: the run executed autonomously under the frozen plan; model calls, prompts, seeds, validator traces, emulator traces, logs, and the artifact manifest are archived in the execution bundle. Model‑call budget and usage: 200 model calls were used (one shared initial generation per task); up to 200 repair calls were allowed but none were applied because initial candidates passed the validator. Human involvement: the human Research Director selected the topic family and pre‑lock constraints; no human manual editing or selective rewriting of technical manuscript content occurred after the autonomy lock. Deviations and restarts: no post‑preregistration design changes or technical restarts occurred. Known reproducibility gap: the randomized holdout selection seed for the Mininet contamination check is not present as a labeled artifact in the archived bundle; this absence prevents deterministic reconstruction of the exact holdout selection despite the contamination summary reporting zero disagreements. The master prompt archive reference above is the immutable prompt required by the track.
limitations: Task‑bank scope: the confirmatory sample used a curated synthetic/public intent→configuration bank (n = 200); results therefore reflect this bank and may not generalize to broader production workloads or adversarial distributions.

Single‑model and shared‑initial setting: only gpt‑5‑mini (hosted) with adapter‑enforced shared‑initial generation was tested (execution artifacts record hosted_model_call_event_count = 200 and stage_counts shared_initial_generation = 200). Outcomes may differ across model families, independent per‑condition sampling, nonzero temperature sampling, or larger repair budgets.

Validator coverage and oracle limitations: the primary deterministic validator enforces a defined set of syntax/intent constraints; validators can fail to capture real device idiosyncrasies, vendor‑specific behaviors, or emergent failure modes detectable only by end‑to‑end deployment.

Adversarial robustness untested: this confirmatory run did not include active adversarial injection or red‑team tool‑description attacks; prior audits indicate such vectors can bypass naive defenses and remain a separate concern.

Reproducibility gap for contamination check: the randomized holdout selection seed for the Mininet contamination check is absent from the labeled artifacts, preventing exact reconstruction of the holdout selection.

Single repair budget: the GVR pipeline allowed at most one automated repair prompt per task; multi‑step repair strategies, different repair budgets, or human‑in‑the‑loop approvals were not exercised here.
